chapter_theme: Marutham: the wife refuses the husband's bard and his excuses, mocking the man who comes in behind their son and sending the go-between back to the other women's street (45, 47-51, 56), laments his false oath (44), and the friend and wife lay the blame on him for his straying, his withheld regard and the 'manliness' he claims (46, 52-55).

43.reading: The woman tells her fair-jewelled friend that those who scold their own kin as simpletons still sit with sealed lips once they have looked the lord of the lotus town in the face; why then should she grieve, when today his chest is known for what it is?
43.nuance: The point seems to be that even the sharp-tongued, who call others fools, fall silent before him, so his charm is no proof against what he does; but lines 3 and 4 are corrupt and the last clause is a guess.

thinai_evidence.note: a lotus-pond town and a quarrel with its lord

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; addressee inferred from the vocative ஏர் மாண்ழாய் (for மாணிழாய்), speaker from the complaint

44.reading: The woman asks her bright-jewelled friend to whom she can say that the lord of the town where bright-petalled lotus buds crowd took her heart and now gives her no thought; long ago she drank in his soft humble words, not knowing they were a false oath.
44.nuance: The complaint looks back from married neglect to the oath of courtship: what betrays her now is not a new act but the discovery that the first words were already false. அச்சுப் பணிமொழி is obscure; 'humble, trembling words' is a guess.

thinai_evidence.note: the lord of the lotus town and the broken oath, a marutham complaint

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: no colophon thurai; addressee from the vocative ஒள்ளிழாய்

45.reading: The speaker says with irony that the lord of the good town is a man of great resource: he comes home carrying their son on his chest, the boy's pearl-strung ornaments crushing the frontlet he wears.
45.nuance: ஆற்றல் உடையன் is praise turned to mockery: his 'strength' is the cunning of coming in behind the child, whom no one can turn away. Line 2 (மேற்றுச் சிறுதாய காய்வஞ்சி போற்றுருவி) is obscure and is not construed here.

thinai_evidence.note: the father uses the son to win entry, the marutham husband's device

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: no colophon thurai; speaker and addressee inferred: the wife comments to her friend on the husband's arrival

46.reading: The woman says she will sit counting it an offence that the lord of the town of wide fields is bound by a garland, but asks why those who have watched his folly should blame the stranger women who show them no friendly face.
46.nuance: She turns the blame from the rival women back on the man: the garland that binds him is his own choosing. The construal of the last two lines is uncertain.

thinai_evidence.note: the husband bound by other women, a marutham quarrel

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: no colophon thurai; speaker inferred from இருப்பன், the addressee from the general question

47.reading: The wife tells the bard, his mouth greasy with meat, that the son has been fed at her breast and she has grown old, so let him go and speak in the street of the women whose breasts are just rising, and eat there, even if he must dance for his meal.
47.nuance: She sets her own body, aged by nursing (மூத்தேம்), against the budding breasts of the street women, and makes the bard a hired dancer who eats where he performs. The opening words போத்தில் கழுத்தில் are hard to construe.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife turns away the husband's bard, the marutham refusal

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: no colophon thurai; the vocative பாண names the addressee

48.reading: The wife tells her bard to leave off speaking of the ways of the lord of the rich good town: let that man of shame keep all that has befallen him, and let the great bard tell what has befallen himself, if anything has.
48.nuance: நாணுடையான், 'the man of shame', is pure irony: the man without shame is given the virtue he lacks, and the bard is invited to talk about anything but his master.

thinai_evidence.note: the bard sent by the husband is told to drop his errand

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: no colophon thurai; the vocatives என்னுடை பாண and இரும்பாண name the addressee

49.reading: The wife tells the bard to lead his master off and tell the flower-like women of the other street what he is: the lord of the cool-ford town, where the red-eyed buffalo that broke its wooden clog sinks into the field pond, gorges on the crop and lies at ease in the shade.
49.nuance: The flower-like women are meant to hear in the buffalo a portrait of the man they are getting.

thinai_evidence.note: the field buffalo and the cool ford

comparisons.tenor: the women of the other street

ullurai.tenor: the husband who has left home for the other women

pairs.situation: he breaks the restraint of his own household
he feeds on what is not his own, the other women
he settles at ease in their houses

ullurai.speaker_fit: the wife uses the buffalo of her own town's fields, a thing she knows (porul 7.26)

50.reading: The wife says it is folly for him to seek entry with the son as his backing: what can they do for the lord of loud revels? Let the bard go on without pause to the street of the gold-like women with flower-filled hair.
50.nuance: ஓவாது செல், 'go without ceasing', tells the bard where his real work lies: he is as much a regular of that street as his master. Line 1 (பேதை புகலை புதல்வன் துணைச்சான்றோன்) is hard to construe.

thinai_evidence.note: the lord of revels and the street of other women, a marutham refusal

comparisons.tenor: the women of the other street

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: no colophon thurai; the vocative பாண names the addressee

51.reading: The wife tells the bard to get up and go, though to speak of the lord of the good pond-town is her own grief: she has as her companion her little son, who every day waves his flawless gold bangles and cries.
51.nuance: துணை closes the poem: the son, not the husband, is named her partner, so the bard's plea has nothing to fill.

thinai_evidence.note: the pond town and the wife who refuses the go-between

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: no colophon thurai; the bard is inferred as addressee from எழுந்தீக and the errand of speaking of the husband

52.reading: The friend asks the lord of the cool-ford town, where the shoal of varaal fish scatters in the drinking pond, whether it is fitting to pass by the bright-bangled wife without a look, leave the house for that street, and call it manliness before the town.
52.nuance: The fleeing fish may hint at the household scattered by his going, as in the long marutham buffalo scenes, but the poem gives only one such match, so it is left as scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the cool ford and the husband's straying

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: no colophon thurai; the vocative ஊர names the hero, the third-person ஒண்டொடி the wife

53.reading: The speaker sets the woman's bewilderment at the deluding words of the lord of the fertile-field town against a pledge: if he comes back having won, as the wheel's rim never misses, she will be one with him through all his days.
53.nuance: Lines 2 and 3 (the bent wheel and its unerring rim) are obscure, and the poem's situation cannot be fixed with confidence.

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: no colophon thurai; speaker and addressee are guesses from நின் வாழ்நாட்கள் and உளேன்

54.reading: The friend tells the lord of the strong-field town, who accepts the wife's devoted service, that if he thinks her merely the gift of the wise elders' wish and resolves to withhold kindly regard from those who do not reckon with him, the blame of it falls on him.
54.nuance: The wife's வழிபாடு (worshipful service) is set against his கண்ணோட்டம் withheld: the poem turns an ethical term into the measure of a husband. The construal of lines 1 and 2 is uncertain.

thinai_evidence.note: field town, and the husband's withdrawn regard

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: no colophon thurai; the second person நின்மேலது names the hero

55.reading: The wife tells the other women not to embrace the lord of the town of loud waters, where the flood crowds in, to the full end of love, nor to pine for him in folly; let them too speak so that their endless longing may leave them.
55.nuance: நீயிரும், 'you too', puts the rivals in the wife's own case: they will be left as she was, so her warning is half scorn and half fellow-feeling.

thinai_evidence.note: the river town and the husband's other women

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: no colophon thurai; the plural imperatives (முயங்கல்மின், ஏங்கல்மின்) and நீயிரும் address the other women

56.reading: The wife says the lord of the town of honey-scented ponds among the fields, letting their flower-eyed son trample and kick him here, praises her slackened breast, while he is the one who presses the budding breasts of his young 'doll'.
56.nuance: தளர்முலை against வளர்முலை: the nursing mother's breast and the girl's rising breast meet in one line, and the domestic scene with the son is exposed as half of a double life. Reading பாவை as the young rival is a guess.

links.note: In Kalittokai 85 the mother shares out her milk in mockery to the 'other mothers' who wept after trusting the father's deceiving oath (மாயச் சூள்); in Ainthinai Ezhupathu 44 a woman says she believed his words long ago, not knowing them for a false oath (பொய்ச்சூள்).
links.teaches: Read together, the false oath is the wound the wife shares with her rivals: Kalittokai's mother pities the other women it deceived, and the venba's speaker finds herself among them, so the oath binds all the man's women in one injury.

links.note: Kalittokai 79: the wife tells the husband not to take up their son, whose hands will pull the pearl chain and garland by which the other women marked him (அணி சிதைப்பான்). Ainthinai Ezhupathu 45: he comes with the son on his chest, the boy's pearl ornaments crushing his frontlet (பட்டஞ் சிதைப்ப).
links.teaches: Kalittokai spells out what the four-line poem only shows: the son's hands spoiling the father's finery are spoiling the other women's tokens, so the venba's ironic 'he is resourceful' means the child he brings as a shield is also the one who exposes him.

links.note: Natrinai 380: refusing the bard, the friend says they smell of ghee, smoke and new birth, holding the son with milk at the breast, and are no match for the man of the bright-jewelled women's street. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 47: the wife says the son is suckled and she is old, and sends the bard to the street of the budding-breasted women.
links.teaches: The pair shows that the nursing mother's body is a set argument in refusing the go-between: the friend in Natrinai offers it as humble unfitness, the wife in the venba turns it into scorn by sending the bard to dance for his food, so the same motherhood can be pleaded as modesty or thrown as contempt.

links.note: Akananuru 46: the friend refusing the husband entry describes his town's red-eyed buffalo breaking its tether in the night, scattering fish and grazing the lotus. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 49: the red-eyed buffalo breaks its wooden clog, eats the field crop and rests in the shade, and the bard is told to carry this to the flower-like women.
links.teaches: The same hidden comparison is aimed at different hearers: in Akananuru 46 it shames the husband at the door, in the venba it is sent through the bard to the other women as a warning, which shows the buffalo ullurai was a portable accusation that could be addressed to either party of the triangle.

links.note: Natrinai 330: the male buffalo plunges into the pond and rests from the day's labour in the sweet shade of the marutham (இன் நிழல் வதியும்), and the friend blames the courtesans' mean hearts. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 49: the buffalo breaks its clog, eats the crop and then rests in the shade (நிழல்வதியும்).
links.teaches: The resting buffalo is innocent after labour in Natrinai and guilty after plunder in the venba, and the blame follows suit, falling on the courtesans in one and on the husband in the other, so what the beast did before the shade decides whom the poem accuses.

links.note: Akananuru 66: the husband, dressed to wed another, is drawn home by the little son who runs to his chariot, and the wife says the old saying about sons has proved true. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 51: the wife sends the bard away, saying her little son with gold bangles is her companion.
links.teaches: The son works on both sides of the marutham quarrel: in Akananuru 66 he pulls the straying father back into the house, in the venba the wife holds him up as companion enough to refuse the father's go-between, so the child is at once the husband's way in and the wife's reason to keep him out.

links.note: Kural 773 calls generous help to a fallen foe (ஊராண்மை) the cutting edge of valour. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 52: the friend mocks the husband for treating his going to the other street as ஊராண்மை, manliness before the town.
links.teaches: The Kural makes ஊராண்மை a virtue of restraint toward the weak, while the friend uses the same word for the husband's public swagger in neglecting his wife, so on a plain reading the two give the word opposite contents, and the venba's sarcasm depends on the higher sense the Kural fixes.

links.note: Kural 572: the world's ways rest on கண்ணோட்டம், and those without it are a burden on the earth. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 54: the husband who resolves to withhold கண்ணோட்டம் while taking the wife's devoted service is told the blame falls on him.
links.teaches: The Kural states kindly regard as a duty of public life; the venba brings it inside the marriage and makes its withdrawal a husband's blame, which shows the ethical term was already at work in the language of domestic quarrel.

links.note: Akananuru 146: refusing the bard, the wife asks who the woman will be who now trusts the deceiving philanderer and will weep and pale as she did. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 55: the wife tells the other women directly not to embrace him to love's end or pine for him, but to give up their longing.
links.teaches: Akananuru 146 only pities the next woman from a distance, while the venba turns to the rivals and counsels them, so together they show the wife's grievance passing into a warning to the women who will suffer as she did.

links.note: Ainkurunuru 65: the wife tells the husband not to embrace her body that bore their son, since it would spoil his chest. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 56: with the son trampling him, he praises her slackened breast, though he presses the budding breasts of a girl elsewhere.
links.teaches: In both the body that bore the son is the ground of the wife's sulking: in Ainkurunuru she withholds it as unfit for his groomed chest, in the venba she sees his praise of it as a cover for his taste for younger bodies, so the mother's body is what she bars him from and what he flatters to come back.

links.note: Kalittokai 85 says the father uses the lying bard as a fishhook to bind the hearts of the women he wants. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 50 tells the bard to go on without pause to the street of the gold-like women.
links.teaches: Kalittokai names the bard as the husband's lure for other women, which explains the venba's order to keep going to that street: the wife is sending the go-between back to his real work, so refusing the bard and accusing him are one act.

source_issues.issue: மாண்ழாய் is probably a misprint for மாணிழாய் (vocative).
மார்(பு)யுஅறிம் is garbled; the line's sense cannot be fixed.
அகன்பனை may stand for அகன்பணை (wide fields); read so here.
மேற்றுச் சிறுதாய காய்வஞ்சி போற்றுருவி is obscure and possibly corrupt.
வளைகிய is unusual (வளைந்த?); lines 2 and 3 cannot be construed with confidence.
